The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) yesterday expressed a desire that I should make a statement with respect to the precise form in which petitions should he drawn, his request having particular reference to a number of documents purporting to be petitions which have recently been handed in.
While it does not seem to me essential that petitioners should use exact or uniform words, it would appear that the practice has invariably been to require substantial adherence to a form- which has long been recognized.
Bourinot, 4th Edition, at page 234, lays down the rule and provides the precedent which should be followed, the first requisite being that every petition should commence wiijh the superscription "To the Honourable The House of Commons in Parliament Assembled." Thus properly addressed and the subject-matter of the petition being in order, it would,still be irregular to receive such a document without a prayer. The practice in the British House of Commons would appear to be substantially the same. May, 11th Edition, at page 525, says: "Without a prayer, a document will not be taken as a petition; and a paper, assuming
ir

the style of a declaration, an address of thanks, or a remonstrance only, without a .proper form of prayer, will not be received."
I have examined a number of the'documents referred to by the hon. member. They are not addressed to the House either in form or in substance. The reference, if to anybody, would appear to be to the Council of the City of Montreal. They contain no prayer. It would appear, therefore, that these documents are not in form and cannot be received.

The word
" prayer " has two meanings, hut I suppose in this case it means a request.
Not the religious meaning.

Mail subsidies and steamship subventions.- Steam service between Canadian Atlantic ports and Australia and New Zealand, $140,000.
[u"I suppose we might as well go on with Estimates tomorrow. I shall go on with my Estimates \u201e 'd some other ministers will be ready, the Minister of Agriculture probably."]

This is in the
hands of the same company as before, the New Zealand Shipping Company.
Are these contracts being carried out at present?

Soime of them are not being carried out to the full. The difficulty of getting vessels is very great and requisitions are frequent. Therefore, sometimes a month is intermitted. We simply pay at the rate provided for each voyage which is completed under the conditions fixed.

From what
port do they sail, and to what ports in Australia and New Zealand?

From Montreal and St. John once monthly, and they have the right to touch at three or four ports in Australia before going on to New Zealand.
Ocean and mail service between Canada and Great Britain, $1,000,000.

Is there any
change in this service?

This service is carried on as last year by the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services. They cannot give what was contracted for when we entered into the arrangement foT the renewed and strengthened service. Such vessels as are approved of, and as can be kept on the Toute under the changes constantly going on orbing to requisition are used. The vessels which have carried on the service during last year and which are relied upon at present chiefly are the Missinabie, the Pretorian, the Grampian, the Metagami, the Scandinavian, the Scotian and the Corsican. These vessels ran in speed from 14 to 15 knots. The service is conducted on a different plane from that originally designed. It is known only at the last moment that such and such a ship will sail, and the

Post Office has to pick it up, generally getting sufficient notice to enable it to forward the mails. Last year the service was performed entirely by boats of the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services, that is, by the old Allan and Canadian Pacific boats. This year, owing to the confused conditions and to the fact that two other lines have come back into the Canadian trade with good boats-the White Star Line and the Cun-ard-we pay so much a trip and take the best vessels of these three lines that offer. The White Star Company have two, the Megantic and the Canada which are very good vessels. The Cunard Company have one or two good vessels and the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services the other vessels. We pay exactly the same rate as we paid last year but on the trip or half trip basis.
Have you, on the whole, the same quantity of tonnage as before?
Not the same amount of tonnage as before the war but a good amount. This year we expect to get two mails each week.
The ports are the same?
Yes.
Has the delivery of the mail been fairly good?

Yes.
Steam service between Canada and Cuba, $25,000.
Was that service performed last year?

No, nor was it performed the year before but it has been allowed to stand because if it becomes possible to continue it, it is a good service for the Maritime Provinces.
Steam service or services between Canada and Newfoundland, $70,000.
This is the same service as last year and at the same rate.
The same company?	.
The same company.	[DOT]
That is a broad statement-between Newfoundland and Canada? Where is that service?

The contract for service is from Sydney to Port aux Basques, hut the same company sails additional boats from Louisburg to St. John direct. They did so last year and they intend

to do so this year. We have contracted for a daily service between Sydney and Port aux Basques connecting with the railway to St. John.

This company do not appear to be able to perform the service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques. We excuse them because of the difficulty they have had in getting ships but I suggested to the minister that before they start a new service from Louisburg to St. Johns the department should insist upon them performing the first service. There is a railway line between Port afix Basques and ,St. Johns and if there is a good line maintained between Port aux Basques and the end of the Intercolonial railway at North Sydney there will be a good service. Before they start a new service, which is rather an unnecessary one, from Louisburg to St. John, because I do not know what particular trade they are going to get, they should improve the present service. Last year and the year before, it was not unusual to see 100, 75, or 50 cars standing on the wharf, waiting for transportation and the excuse was that they had no boats. I call this to the attention of the minister and I would suggest that he should insist upon the company doing as much as possible to supply a fairly good service between Port aux Basques and North Sydney before they try to get boats for what would appear to be an unnecessary service.

That is entirely within the option of the company. We have no orders to give in that respect. Our contract for service is between Port aux Basques and Sydney. The vessels are not diverted from that route to the service between Placentia and Louisburg. The company have other vessels for that service. I mentioned it to show that the same company, which was performing the service between Sydney and Port aux Basques, were making occasional trips between Louisburg and Placentia. Originally the boats were excellent ones but were both taken off the route, a year and a half or two years ago. One was taken by the Allies for work in northern Russia and I think the other was sold to the same power with the consent of the Government as they se'emed to be needed by Russia. The vessels which were on a year ago and which are on now had a bigger cargo carrying capacity than the original boats. Freights are going and they go every day. Mails are being carried and they are being carried every day. The quality, appearance and passen-

ger accommodation of these boats are not quite so good as those of the boats that were previously on. For this diminution in character a reasonable deduction is made from the amount of the subsidy.

I am not suggesting that the minister should make any deductions because I believe it is very difficult for the company to get boats and the service is a very good one and is affording great facilities for trade between Newfoundland and Canada via North Sydney. The minister says the service is from Sydney. It is not from Sydney and if it is so on the books of the minister's department it is a mistake. The service is from North Sydney.
It is from Greater Sydney.

Yes, the commercial
metropolis of Eastern Canada.
Quite so.

We must aim to get other facilities in connection with this trade as well as supplying the boats, or encouraging the company to supply boats. There are several other things in connection with the trade that the ministers who perhaps should look after them, are neglecting. The building of a wharf possibly belongs to the department of Public Works and taking it over and looking after it is possibly the duty of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, but to afford facilities for trade, it would seem to come under the direction of the Department of Trade and Commerce. If these other ministers should try to get clear of their responsibilities, in this matter we must look to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. At North Sydney, where connection is made by steamboat between Canada and Newfoundland and where the Intercolonial ends, tRe wharf is absolutely inadequate for the business which has to be handled there.
The buildings on this wharf come right to the edge on one side, so that there is berthing accommodation for only one steamer. A steamer lies there every day so that there is no room for fishing vessels to transfer their cargoes to the railway cars at this wharf, and they are obliged to go to a private wharf and have the fish trucked to a railway car. Then complaint is made that the railway arrangements are such that only one car can be handled at a time. We have a magnificent harbour, and it would be very easy to extend the wharf so as to
give sufficient berthing accommodation for all vessels. I brought this matter to the attention of the acting Minister of Railways last year, but nothing has been done. I know it is useless to bring it to the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as he simply collects wharfage on wharves that have been completed. I therefore urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), whose duty it is to see that facilities are provided for our people to carry on trade and commerce, to urge his colleagues to provide sufficient money to make proper acommodation for the carrying on of business by our people.
I noticed the otheT day a newspaper statement that a large increase had been made in the subsidy for this steam service to Newfoundland.
The information is not correct.
What was the subsidy paid that company five years ago compared with that paid to-day?
The subsidy is as stated here. The vote is $70,000. Five years ago, that is 1912, we paid $31,874. In 1915 it was $48,000, and this year about the same.

So that the statement
is correct?	[DOT]

In speaking of an increase, I thought it meant a modern increase, not one of ancient years. One very important difference is that formerly this company was paid in addition $30,000 as a postal subsidy. That is not now paid, and it is now a daily service.
Is this service to Louis-burg something new, or the occasional trips to that port during the winter months?

I think thie is
winter's months trips.
Steam service between Canada and the West Indies or South America, or both, $34.0,666,66.

Has the minister any
figures to give us as to the treaty with the West Indies? Has there been an increase in our trade as a result of the treaty?

Yes, I think I may say there has been a very satisfactory increase. In 1912, the value of cargoes of Canadian origin going over this line was $2,325,000. In 1914, it was $2,618,000. In
1915,	it was $3,507,000, and last year, in
1916,	it was $4,698,000. Thus, comparing

1912 and 1916, the value of Canadian cargoes has a little more than doubled. Of course, you have to take into account that prices have risen in that time, but still it shows a very gratifying increase. Then there is Some little carriage of goods of United States origin.
Is there a large increase in imports?
The chief increase is in exports. But last year, and partly the yeaT before, there was a very large increase in imports owing to the very large amount of sugar brought in for the refineries.
What are the chief imports?
The chief articles imported are the tropical products, sugar, coffee, eocoanut, Trinidad asphalt, oranges and bananas.
And our exports?

Our exports run over the whole gamut of our natural products, such as fish, canned salmon, canned goods, flour, oats, vegetables, groceries, cheese, pease, live-stock, sulphate of ammonia, tea, fertilizer, lumber, laths, cordage, and a great many other articles.
Has my hon. friend any figures in regard to potatoes?
I have not them here. I can get a statement in regard to them.
I understand the minister to say that the value of the goods imported during the last three or four years has doubled.
The exports have about doubled.

I suppose we rftay also assume that the freight collected by the steamers has doubled. I think, as a matter of fact, it has more than doubled. It would appear to an outsider, if my surmise is true, that the subsidy in this case might be reduced, because if they were able, in 1912, to carry on a successful business and pay dividends on half the trade they should he able now, as they are getting more than twice as much money, to carry on business with a less subsidy. My idea is that these subsidies 'are given for the purpose of building up a trade. [DOT] Once the trade is built up, so that it becomes self-sustaining, we should not continue paying the same amount of

subsidy. We should have a system by which the subsidy would be reduced and applied somewhere else.

I have had a long experience in connection with the running of the service between Canadian ports and the West Indies. When I was in the ministry many, many years ago, we began this service, and I think I can safely say that no West Indian service which has ever been run between Canada 'and the West Indies has been a paying proposition. My hon. friend knows, probably better than I, the extreme difficulties of a West Indian service to be found in the character of their ports, only one or two of them allowing Vessels to get up to dock. They have a system of lighterage everywhere, and long distances between the ports, and an itinerary which takes about six weeks to make, and, in addition to all these things, we have a not over-abundant passenger list, which is, of course, the paying part in such a service. I think I can say, without any doubt, that the line which is now carrying on the service is the best that we ever had, and the service is entirely satisfactory from the point of view of what is attainable and what is advisable between our country and the West Indies. Some parties advocate a faster service, a 15, 17 or 18 knot service, mainly for passengers. Others advocate cargo boats alone. These boats in use now are a cross between the cargo boat and the passenger boat. They have excellent passenger accommodation and good cargo accommodation, and1 the two combine very well on these steamers, I think that very general satisfaction has been given by the work which is done with them. In reference to the reduction of the subsidy, we keep as close a tab as possible upon the rates, and no rates are 'raised without the authority of the department, and an investigation is always made before any advance is allowed. The expenses of steamships, as my hon. friend knows, have very greatly increased, and last year and the year before-particularly last year-the expenses were very heavily increased. There has been a very great increase in the price of coal, and on these long voyages a tremendous amount of coal is used. The size of the coal bill for these vessels is astonishing. I have tried to keep in touch with the Halifax and St. John Boards of Trade in reference to the control and regulation of the rates which have been paid, and we have always arrived, I think, at a satisfactory conclusion, after discussion, in regard to freight rates. When one thinks

of what would happen if these vessels were taken off, it makes one prize the service more. We have a pretty severe struggle to keep those vessels on the route, and within the last three or four weeks they came very close to being requisitioned, owing to the necessities of the Mother Country, but we have been able to keep them on. If they were thkem off at tfhis Ipartdcular juncture, it would practically cut off connections between Canada and the West Indies.

I am quite aware that
the business is abnormal just now, and that it is very difficult to find vessels to do any kind of work. I am glad to know that the minister is keeping track of the rates, and endeavouring to control them in some way, but if the minister has the information at hand, it would be interesting to the' committee to hear about the rates on some special articles, as they existed in 1912 and as they exist to-day, so that we may have some idea of the increase that has taken place.

I have not the figures with me, but, will be very glad to secure them. My hon. friend will see, all things considered, that there has not been the increase that he might fear on the staple articles. The rates on flour and staple goods have been kept down very well. The Tates on sugar, molasses, and one or two other articles, have been increased, but they have been able to bear the increase.

Perhaps you can furnish us with that information. I know the rates on the tramp steamers from the West Indies on molasses and sugar have increased very much, and I should like to know how they compare with the rates on the steamers to which we are paying subsidies.

That is a difficult question to answer, because the tramp steamer takes whatever she can get. If somebody wants a cargo, moved, and the tramp steamer is able to move it, if it is a case of necessity, almost any rate will be given. We can compare the rates on our steamers with the rates on the steamers from New York. In no case do our rates exceed-and in most cases they are lower- than the rates from New York.

During the last year or
two I have heard earnest appeals from Canadians who visit the West Indies at various times and who take an interest in trade matters, who feel that the time is now
opportune to bring about reciprocity between Canada and the West Indies, as a result of the war. Has anything been done of an official character? Is the minister in a position to know if any feeling has been manifested in regard to this matter among our fellow citizens in Canada?
That isf a kind of rapproachement.

That is the suggestion I
have read under the signature of very able correspondents in the Montreal press. Mr. Macaulay, of Montreal, thought it would be an opportune time, and I wanted to inquire if any move had been made in that regard, or if the matter is still the subject of academic discussion.

Mr. Macaulay has written some very excellent articles, and is a very firm believer in a closer connection than a commercial connection with the West Indian islands. I have my own thoughts about that, but I have not put them before the public, because I think it is a great deal better that the West Indian islands should come to us rather than that Canada should take the position of seeking to influence sentiment in the West Indies. This much I know, that there is a growing friendly sentiment between the two countries induced by intercommunication, and a very excellent influence in that direction has been the extension of the banking facilities of Canada to the West Indian islands, and the increase of. trade and personal communication. The extension of the banks to the West Indies has been a cogent argument and a plain proof of how much export trade depends upon banking facilities which emanate from Canada as an exporting country. The lesson that has been learned from what is going on in the West Indies is a very excellent one for our exporters. I have my own opinion that in the extension of trade which is to come after this, one of the potent influences for that extension will be the influence of inter-related banking facilities. There are, of course, questions that have to be taken into consideration when any union between the West Indies and Canada is considered. Those will not be insuperable, maybe, when the proper time comes for discussing such matters.

I am glad that my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has brought this question to the notice of the committee. For several years past I have read very able articles by Mr. Macaulay, of

the Sun Life Assurance.Company, who has long been the chief exponent of the idea of union between the West Indies and Canada. No doubt the West Indies, since the construction of the Panama canal, have become of great strategic value to the British Empire. The United States have lately acquired one of the Danish islands, which shows that they have an eye open to the business that will necessarily accrue in the future as a result of the construction of the Panama canal. There have been 4 p.m. objections raised to the scheme of bringing the West India islands into our Confederation. Some years ago, in my official capacity, I attended a conference in London, that question was discussed in my presence by two of the then members of the Campbell-Bannerman Government. One of them said en passant: "The United States Government have their colour problem; do you think that the Dominion of Canada would absorb the West Indies with the colour question looming up so seriously in the neighbouring republic?" My object in rising when I heard my hon. friend (Mr. Marcil) inquiring about the proposed union of the West Indies with Canada, was to speak of that other union scheme which I think is much more feasible and much more practical and urgent. I refer to the union of Newfoundland with Canada. I am travelling perhaps far afield from the item under discussion, but my remarks will not be lengthy. I understand that for the last four or five years the objection in Newfoundland against the idea of union with Canada has lost some of its force. We all know that the late Archbishop Howley had succeeded in influencing public opinion very largely in favour of the idea of an ultimate union between Newfoundland and Canada. Since then-and I wish to draw the attention of the minister particularly to this point-I understand that overtures have been made to Canada, and that there has been a voluminous correspondence on the subject between the present Prime Minister of Newfoundland and 'the Prime Minister of Canada. The facts were made public not long ago in the Montreal papers as a result of litigation between the owner of a certain paper and one of its former editors. There it was " alleged that negotiations had recently taken place between the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland, and that the question of union between the ancient colony and the Dominion had been seriously entertained. What truth is there in those allegations or' rumours, and has a scheme of union between Newfoundland 
and Canada been contemplated by the Government?

I think my hon. friend has, in his excursion, travelled so far away from the item under discussion that he has rather confused my tabula. I am now intent entirely on commercial ocean services, and my attention is given so completely to that, that I beg my hon. friend not to switch me off this afternoon. One remark that T made with reference to the West Indian matter to my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), I will repeat to my hon. friend, and follow it up with the simple saying that so far as Canada is concerned, with reference to Newfoundland, our latch-string is always on the outside and a light is always burning in the window.

Some time ago I brought to the attention of the House the fact that salt was extremely scarce for carrying on the fisheries in the Maritime Provinces. The fishermen have responded to the appeal for greater production. We have a prolific fishery and active fishermen, but it is impossible to carry on the business successfully without an ample supply of salt, and owing to the scarcity of tonnage the shortage of salt is becoming alarming. I understand that the department has taken up this question, and I should like to know whether the minister has succeeded in getting tonnage for carrying salt to Halifax and other ports in the Maritime Provinces.

My department has been dealing with this question for about four or five months, and the result is simply this. The reason I speak of it is that freight rates on the Atlantic route are said to have risen to enormous proportions. Apart altogether from the question of building ships, I suggest to my hon. friend the possibility of securing a freight steamship service, or even a service by sailing vessels, between ports in the Maritime Provinces and those of the United States which are close to the coal supply. It seems to me a most extraordinary, a most deplorable, thing that the cost of anthracite coal in St. John has reached the enormous price of $15 per ton. It is a matter of very great importance and I invite the attention of the minister to it. These are times when departures must be made from the rules which govern under normal conditions. In normal times there was an abundance of vessel accommodation available. To-day there are scarcely any available for the coastal service.

Yes, that is very true but the other remark my hon. friend made is equally true that there is a deplorable scarcity of transport tonnage. I do not know at the present time where a single vessel can be got for a subsidy to run on these coasts. We have tried from below New York to Maine and New Brunswick. That is the result of the war and the circumstances will not, in .so far as I can see, be mitigated during this season. I think transport iwill be more and more difficult to get during this season. At the end of this season, and during next season, there will be a very considerable contribution of new tonnage which will gradually come in. But little of that will come in until the latter part of this season. The year 1918 will, I think, see a pretty large addition. The difficulty is that the new vessels which are being built are being built largely for the Imperial Government under contract with the Imperial Munitions Board. They will be used upon the Atlantic but that will not help out the local situation. My hon. friend admits that the situation is very grave indeed. Why would it not be a good thing for the Government to engage in the building of a hundred small wooden vessels in the Maritime Provinces and in Quebec and put them on the trade routes? Let the Government control these boats and keep down the transportation rates by means of them. These small vessels, of 250 or 400 or 500 tons, could be built very quickly in the Maritime Provinces. I have scores of letters from people who say that shipyards are available, timber could be got, and men put to work. But it is said the Imperial Government does not believe in these smaller vessels, and have limited the size to 2,500 tons. All the better, let the Imperial Government go on through the Imperial Munitions Board building the larger vessels, but let the Dominion Government engage in the building of smaller vessels which apparently there will be no danger of the Imperial Government commandeering. Then they will be available for encouraging local trade. The situation, as the minister has said, is grave. I say its gravity cannot be magnified; it is very grave indeed. I believe that unless some relief is given coal will actually run to $20 a ton. See what a burden it is upon the people, upon the families of the soldiers who have gone to the front to fight the battles of the Empire. How serious will be the burden upon them and upon all classes of the community! The Government can give relief if it wants to and if it will take hold of the question in a reasonable and proper manner, as it ought to have begun to do two years ago. The Government ought to have anticipated the very condition that exists to-day. The war may run on for two or three years longer; that is the opinion of men in England and in the United States who ought to know; and are we simply to lie down and to do nothing except to deplore the situation and express the opinion that it will grow worse as the months and years go by? Surely, instead of talking about it, something practical ought to be done. If the Government took hold of the situation in a practical way, so far as the coal transportation in Canada is concerned, I believe that very satisfactory ' results could be obtained within a year. It is very late, I admit, but it is not tdo late.
In view of the conditions to which our people must look forward in the near future,
I say it will be nothing less than a crime if this Government does not take measures in the emergency which has arisen in respect

to transportation between ports in Canada, and between p.orts in the United States and in Canada.

There is a principle involved in what my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has said that is more important and wider even than the geographical country of which he is speaking. I think it is an important principle which he enunciated, that these unfortunate conditions should, so far as possible, be foreseen and anticipated. It is only thus that you will provide against them in the most economic way. If the Government simply, in an easy-going way, drag along and say, We can get along this week and this month, and all through the summer without coal in the Maritime Provinces and on the prairies, it may have quite an easy existence in the interim, but the condition of affairs when the crisis really comes upon the different parts of the country will be a great deal more grave even than if it were anticipated and provided for as far as possible. We know that the Government has many pressing matters calling for its attention *which are affairs of the moment, but it is just as important that they should sit down in an intelligent way and look into the future and endeavour to solve the problems of the future by preparedness, as to think about the things that are urgent for the moment. The whole story of good legislation is the anticipation of the future and providing against its troubles. The trouble we have to-day owing to the shortage of men for overseas service might have been anticipated and prepared for, and we might have avoided the crisis that stares our nation in the face at the moment, if the Government had looked intelligently into the future and had foreseen, as they could have foreseen, what now is clear to every person. They might have foreseen it long ago.
I remember that three years ago this Government had as part of its duty the providing of seed for the western farmers. They had all winter to provide the seed, but nothing at all was done. They waited until spring came, and then they had to pay, not quite double, but nearly double what they would have had to pay if the seed had been purchased when the price was more reasonable. I think the Government then went out and bought seed at $1.50 a bushel which the homesteaders had to pay. They paid that for the very same wheat that they could have purchased some months before for less than $1 a bushel.

We have a condition of affairs in the western provinces which is more grave and vital than the condition to which my hon. friend has referred. On the prairies we have a class of people who have no other source of fuel than coal. We have been accustomed to get enormous quantities of Pennsylvania coal, and we have also received coal from the western collieries, particularly those at Lethbridge and Drumheller. As I said, the Pennsylvania coal is to be cut,off this year, and we will not have it next year at all. The best judges of the coal situation tell us that practically no Pennsylvania coal will be brought into the prairie provinces next year, and we all know that we cannot have coal in the winter from the western coal mines unless coal is mined during the spring and summer. The Government seem to be handling this question in the same easy-going manner. We have asked time and time again what has been done and what is being done in the way of anticipating what will be a crisis in this nation when there is a failure of coal supplies from the United States and the western mines to provide fuel to keep our people warm on the prairies. The matter has not yet become one of life and death, but the fact that the crisis is somewhat removed in time does not detract one iota from its certainty. So surely as time is marching on, so surely will that real, physical condition of affairs come upon us, and that grave crisis present itself when the summer is past and the months for consuming coal are really with us. We have been at the Minister of Labour for weeks and weeks to know what he is doing. We do not know whether the minister realizes the gravity of the situation or not. We very much doubt if, for a moment, he realizes its gravity in such a way as a statesman should, and I think that the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) is doing absolutely the right thing in impressing upon the Government that it is their duty to anticipate problems and crises of this kind. The only economic way, the only statesmanlike way, of providing against these problems and crises, is to look at them in ample time and make some provision in the way-of preparedness before the crisis is really upon us. I say this with a great deal of seriousness. The condition of affairs in our western country is one that no man can contemplate without the utmost seriousness. We have had the Pennsylvania supply cut off; and in our own western coal districts, between the Minister of Labour and the operators and the Coal Miners'

Union, -there is nothing but chaos; they are doing everything but producing coal. . The minister is digging up excuses by the top, but no coal is being dug. Under these circumstances, the Government is not discharging its great duty to the people, that is to do something to prevent this very grave and vital crisis from facing us. I have known winters in the West when the Northwest Mounted Police have been scouring the prairies-we do not like to mention these things in this House-going to this shack and that shack, this district and that district, and finding men- who had suffered death because they h"d not fuel to keep themselves warm.
I speak for the homesteaders, the women and the little children on those prairies. The Minister of Labour should not merely say: " For the present there is no crisis, no one is cold; we will cross the bridge when we come to it," but I think he should, as the hon. member from St. John advocated, anticipate the future, and say that these precious days and-months shall not slip by, but that something shall be done under the circumstances, so that this impending crisis may be -averted. I speak of this -as a national affair. You cannot encourage people to continue living on those prairies in the West if you do nothing to avert a crisis such as is threatened. We want the people to stay there, develop the country and produce wealth on the unimproved prairie land. Therefore, the Government must discharge its duties and make living possible in that country. I urge the minister and the Government to anticipate these matters and address themselves to it, and no-t remain idle day after day, and say they do not know of the conditions. Apparently they have done nothing, and I think that they should, after thoughtful consideration, come to this Chamber and say they are going to do something. They cannot do much by commission. We have had commissions until we -are tired of them. A -commission was -appointed a year and a half ago to deal with the resources of Canada. They were going to knit everything together in a beautiful web, everything would work economically, and each industry would minister to the resources of the other industries. They held a few meetings, and we heard no more of them for some months. I am not hopeful of commissions. I s-ay nothing about the appointment o-f Mr. M*agrath. The hour has not come to discuss his fitness; my mind is open; I have not decided one way or -the other on that, but we cannot conclude that the responsibility is shelved, -and the Government's duty fulfilled simply because Mr. Magrath has been appointed. The House and the country should be informed as to wh-at is -being done to avert the grave condition of affairs which is threatened, and the matter is not far removed from the subject under discussion. The minister might tell us whether the appointment of Mr. Magrath is all that he purposes doing, or whether he is still going to devise something which will have practical results in saving us from the grave conditions which threaten us through shortage of fuel in the West.

I have no desire to
withhold anything from the committee which I think, in the public interest, should be divulged. My hon. friend from Moose-jaw probably appreciates the difficulty that we had to overcome in the southeasterly part of British Columbia, and the southwesterly part of Alberta. This is -not the only difficulty that has existed out there. There were serious strikes in 1903, 1906, and 1907, and a more serious one in 1909, extending over five months. Another, still more -serious, occurred in 1911, extending over eight months. * I have no desire to find any fault with my predecessor. I have no doubt he did everything he could to avert these labour disturbances in that district. We have been exceptionally successful since the autumn of 1911, till a few months ago, and had no difficulties in that district. We first made an agreement in October 1911 for some three years and four months, which continued until March, 1915, when another agreement was entered into, to continue for two years from that date. That agreement worked satisfactorily till July last. At that time the workers declared that they would not adhere to the provisions of the agreement any longer, although it would not expire till the 31st March of this year. They then demanded a war bonus of ten per cent increase over and above the provisions of the agreement of 1915. The operators, in substance, conceded that demand. It was not a flat increase of ten per cent all round, but it ran from 7J to 12 per cent, or from five to twelve and a half per cent, and the miners, under that arrangement and a sub sequent one, continued to work. The last agreement, as the former one, provided that thirty days before its expiration, the two bodies should get together, -and endeavour to negotiate an agreement, so that there would be no cessation of work when that

agreement expired. They came together in March and negotiated for seven weeks, and finally reached an agreement satisfactory to the representatives of the men and the operators, but, under the constitution of the United Mine Workers of America, no such agreement could be effective until a vote of the men themselves was taken. That vote was taken about May 5, and the men rejected the agreement that their representatives had negotiated, and quit work. We have been making every effort to secure a resumption of work in those mines. I have not gone into the details of what was done. I do not think it would be in the public interest to do so now. We are just as anxious about it as the hon. gentleman from Moosejaw is, and we are giving it very close attention. I have no doubt that whatever means may be necessary to accomplish the object, those mines will resume operation irf .a very short time. The Government prefer the owners should operate these mines under an amicable arrangement with the miners. If that cannot be done, other means will be adopted to operate the mines. I do not think it is necessary for me to give details of what is being done at the present time, but I will assure the committee that work will be resumed just as soon as possible, and I expect it will be within a very short time.

I expect to go to my riding in the very near future. Inasmuch as I should be informed of what has happened here, the first thing the people will ask me will be: "Did not the Minister of Labour, a number of weeks ago, say that, if the operators and tne miners did not co-operate, the Government would see that the mines were operated?" or words to that effect. I will have to answer that the minister did use words to that effect a few weeks ago. They will askWhat would the natural meaning of the words of the minister be, as understood by an impartial listener; would it not mean that matters would be remedied in much less time than has really elapsed?" We worry about the matter of time, because it is tremendously important to us, as the minister will appreciate. I accepts his statement now. There is not much trouble to-day but the time will come when it will be, not only a matter of comfort but of saving human life, and they will say: "Did not the minister give you to understand that, if the mine owners and others did not co-operate, he would do something, and was not the impression that the minister gave that that promise or statement would be carried into effect without the lapse of time which has

already occurred without considering the delay which may take place in the future."

I will take my hon.
friend further into my confidence and give him the information which I had at that time. The president of the Mine Workers of America, which is an international labour *organization, having its headquarters at Indianapolis, sent me a message stating that he had sent to the president-of the organization in district 18 a telegram the substance of which is as follows: I have instructed the men to return to work immediately on conditions obtaining on the 31st of March last, and as soon as we get through with the convention I am attending here in Minneapolis, I will either go myself or send representatives to the district to endeavour to reach an agreement satisfactory to both parties. When I stated in the House that I expected the men to return to work within forty-eight hours, I had that telegram in my possession, and I believed the local officers would at once carry out the instructions given by the president of the organization. Within a few days the representatives of the men sent me a message giving me a copy of one which they said they had sent to the president of the organization telling him that they were going to manage the matter for themselves and that he should not interfere. That was rather a peculiar stand for the men to take. Mr. White, however, the president of the International organization, took the matter up with the local officers at each mine throughout the whole district, which is a very large one, and he endeavoured through them to have the men return to [DOT]work at once. That endeavour appears to have failed also. I received a message yesterday stating that I would have some definite information to-day, but I have not received anything yet. We are keeping *close watch on the matter, and I can only *assure my hon. friend that we are not losing sight of the importance of having coal for the farmers, for transportation purposes, and for the purpose of keeping smelters at work in order that manufacturers of muni-itions in the different factories throughout the country may continue operations. I believe that very soon work will be resumed in those mines.

Both the Minister of Labour and the hon. member for Moosejaw are good friends of mine, and I am glad to see them occasionally, but they have come into my house and turned me out. I have let them have a period for

cavorting around and honours, I think, are now about equal, so that I suggest that we go back to the work before the committee.

No. The Panama canal from which a great deal was expected, and still is expected, has not developed the through trade that was expected, owing to some difficulties in the canal itself, but more particularly owing to the war.

There have been statements that wheat passing through the Panama canal would be in danger of fermentation. British Columbia looked forward hopefully to the development of trade on the opening of the canal. Some time ago I saw a very large elevator there which had been built for the handling of wheat, but had been very little used. Has the department considered the possibility of fermentation of wheat passing through the tropics?

The department, of course, has no experience with wheat passing through the canal, but we do not expect any difficulty such as my hon. friend suggests. Wheat from Argentina moves through equatorial areas and reaches Britain in good shape. My own opinion is that there would be no difficulty in this respect, but the question will not be settled, I suppose, until the cargoes go through.

I am glad to hear that the minister is of that opinion; it is my own view. There should be no danger of fermentation, as wheat from the Argentine and other countries passes through the same zone and arrives in Britain in good condition.

There is always this to be taken into account: Wheat raised in different countries, and even in different parts of the same country, varies greatly in the degree of moisture it contains. That has been exemplified in our own Northwest. About three years ago, taking up the question of the future transportation of wheat with a view to the lines which that transportation would permanently follow, I established in Winnipeg a laboratory in charge of Dr. Birchard, where experiments have been, and still are, carried on, to ascertain the moisture contents* at different seasons, of the wheat grown in different parts of the Northwest and the keeping qualities of the wheat under transit conditions. Records of these experiments are carefully kept, and so we are building up a basis for general conclusions in Tegard to *such matters as the use of the Panama canal for the transport of our wheat. As

the temperature conditions will be about the same-certainly no worse-for the Panama canal transit for our wheat and the present transit for Argentine wheat, I venture the opinion that there will be no difficulty on that account.

Steam service from the opening to the closing of navigation in 1917 between the mainland and Magdalen Islands, $18,000.

The minister is
aware that this is a very poor and unsatisfactory service. The directors and managers of the steamer employed in this service openly discriminate, in their own favour, against other people doing business. The fact of the matter is that while the "Lady Sybil" was on this service, the "Amelia" was also employed at the work she is doing to-day, namely, carrying goods for her owners, the difference being that she is now being paid a subsidy by the Government. I had occasion to call the attention of the department to a glaring instance of discrimination, which took place last fall, of which I have personal knowledge. Some parties in the Magdalen islands in the fishing business

and I suppose rivals to some extent in business with the owners of this ship-bought some boat plank from the firm with which I am associated. When we were shipping this plank, the captain told us he had no room and could not take it. The owner's boat builder happened to be present, and he offered to buy the plank. Under the circumstances we were delighted to sell it, and immediately space was found for it on the steamer, and because, in doing my duty, as a member of Parliament, I drew the attention of the department to this fact and to other facts of which I was aware, these people refused to pay for the plank, and the consequence will be a lawsuit.
You should not have complained till you got your money?

But, as a public man,
I had a duty to discharge.
Duty is imperative.
What is the name of the owner of the vessel?

William Leslie & Co. are large owners, and Robert Leslie & Co. are part owners. Dr. Starrat is the manager representing the firm of Robert Leslie & Co. I know that parties in the Magdalen islands cannot import goods unless they have the good will of these people. They are penalized, and they have no certainty that their goods will be carried. It is an intolerable state of affairs.
What is the name of the . boat?

The "Amelia." Last /ear a lumber-laden steamer was wrecked in the gulf of St. Lawrence. This, boat went to the rescue, but it was after tugs powerful enough to take the disabled steamer to Halifax had arrived; the "Amelia" was doing very little work, and her services could have been dispensed with. I am informed that the manager, Dr. Starrat,. was remonstrated with for having the steamer off the route for such a length of time, and he stated that he did not care whether he received the subsidy or not, because he expected his share of the salvage would be larger than the subsidy the Government would pay. The service was interrupted for a considerable time in that way, without any necessity whatever. I called the attention of the department to this last year, and I thought possibly some reduction would be made in the subsidy, on account of the very inefficient service, and on account, particularly, of the discriminatiori against the ordinary business man, but no penalty was enforced, and they were not obliged to make any refund. Conditions this year are worse. The company appear now to realise that they can do just what they like, and yet this large subsidy is being paid. This condition of affairs is intolerable. When the contract with the Lady Sybil expired, Mr. William McLure, the owner of the ship, was willing to enteT into a new contract with the -department for a number of years, but the department refused to renew the contract for more than one year. If that be the case, it was poor business judgment on the part of the department because ships were becoming scarcer every year and it would be an advantage for the department to enter into a contract for some years. Mr. McLure, knowing that he could not get a contract for more than one year, received and accepted a good offer for his ship, and the result is the inefficient service we have today. Surely the department is not powerless; surely this company will not be allowed to do just as they please; surely the department will not pay them $18,000 a year of the public money for practically carrying their own goods and discriminating against those of nearly everyone else. It. would be almost a good thing to abolish this service, because the public are receiving no good whatever, and the company feel their position so strong that any one who calls attention to this matter is likely to be penalized. Surely the minister can do something to mitigate this crying injustice.

Last year I informed the minister that the Amelia was quite inadequate to the service and was a dangerous boat to travel on. The same boat is still on the service, and I have received from my former electors in the Magdalen islands many protests against the service. There is no space in the boat available for passengers and the boat is very filthy. The Lady Sybil was built especially for the service; she was run for a year or two by the Leslie company, and then that company thought it more advantageous to put that boat elsewhere and to put on the Amelia. Finally the Lady Sybil was sold to Mr. McLure, and she gave a most excellent service to the Magdalen islands. It would be a pity if the inhabitants of those islands, who are isolated for such a long period of the year, should suffer through the action of the department. The minister should look into the matter again and see that those people receive a better service.

If I could have lived up to the difficult task set for me this afternoon by the hon. member for Mooee-jaw, and known five years ago what was going to happen to-day, I might have made different dispositions', but that was a pretty difficult thing to do. I tried to get the loan of a boat from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, but it was impossible for him to accommodate me, and in the end the Amelia was the only boat available and I had to take her. I do not think we could have done without this service to the Magdalen Islands. She was paid therefor $14,000, there being a reduction on account of services not performed. The same condition of affairs prevails this year; there is no other boat available.
With reference to what the hon. member for Prince Edward Island said, this is the first I have heard of the difficulties which occurred last year, and I shall certainly look into the matter. A steamboat owner who
is paid to perform a public service certainly should not discriminate in favour of his own business or between two persons whose freight he carries, and I should be loath to think that that had been done. But ae the hon. member has brought the matter to my attention I will make inquiries, and if the information is different from what he says I will inform him and the committee.

Would the minister instruct his inspector to see that the boat is kept in a sanitary condition? From the complaints I received last fall from a clergyman on the Islands it certainly looks as if the inspector had failed in his duties. How many times a year does the inspector look over these subsidized boats?
He visits them all once during the season; that is the utmost he can do.
I know it is difficult to get a suitable boat for this service, but I wish the minister would make a special point of seeing that this boat is kept in a clean and sanitary condition.

Had the minister
followed my advice about this service two or three years ago we would not be in the position we are in to-day. The minister will recall that I urged the desirability of giving such a^subsidy as would secure the services of the Lady Sybil. The eastern portion of Prince Edward Island and the Magdalen Islands may be an isolated place, but they are inhabited by the very best Canadian citizens, and it is very important that a good service should be given them, ilf the Lady Sybil had been engaged all this trouble would have been avoided. There is no question about the unfitness of the Amelia for carrying passengers and performing the service generally in a proper way. I have not personal knowledge of the conditions mentioned by my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island, but I have heard rumours of complaints along the line indicated, and I think the minister should look into the matter.

The Prince
Edward service is to be carried on by the Intercolonial railway. I have not exact information on that subject. I understand from the report of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) and from his statements in the House, that everything is now fitted for running and that the improvements contemplated will be made before the season of navigation is over, so that this new route will be in use through the winter season. As to the concentration of the service at that point, and as to what is taking place on the old route, I am not able to give my hon. friend the information. There will be some dislocation and it may be some hardship to localities, until the trade accommodates itself to the new route. But, on the whole, the balance of advantage ought to be with the new and improved ferry route.

Do I understand the minister to say that during the present summer it is expected that the Department of Railways will manage communication with Prince Edward Island by the ferry between Cape Tormentine and Cape Traverse?
That is what I understood.
And the route from Summerside to Pointe du Chene, and Pictou to Charlottetown, will be done away with? Is that the hon. gentleman's impression?

I hope the hon. gentleman is wrong. Some department of the

Government own boats which are still fitted for service on the present route. And, as the Prince Edward Island railway is not of standard gauge, to concentrate traffic at one point by means of a car ferry seems an outrageous proposition.
These boats may be running; I am not sure. All I know is that the railway is looking after the service.

The Minister of
Trade and Commerce is much more familiar with the geography of that portion of the country than is the Minister of Railways.
Yes, I know the geography.

I can tell the hon. minister that it is the opinion of people in close touch with the business that goes on between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, men whose opinions are worth something, that the oar ferry, run under present conditions, that is with a narrow guage railway on Prince Edward Island, will never take care of all the traffic. Besides that, a large portion of the Island traffic is with eastern Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. To carry produce from the eastern end of Prince Edward Island by car ferry to the eastern portion of Nova Scotia is much the same in principle, though not quite in degree, as to go fr.om Ottawa to Liverpool by way of Vancouver and Montreal. If the minister can use his influence with the Minister of Railways to allow the boats to run at least this summer between Pdctou and Charlottetown and Pointe du Chene and Summer-side, until the car ferry is tested, I think that would be only reasonable.

I shall be glad
to see my colleague on that subject.

The Minister of Railways is a very difficult man to get anything out of. It is very difficult to find out what he is doing. He is not like the Minister of Trade and Commerce who, I am bound to say, is genial and willing to give information.
Don't draw comparisons, please.
I hope the hon. gentleman will not be offended seeing that the comparison is favourable to him. I am going to appeal to him as an old Maritime Province man

That is where
you hit me on a tender point.

-to have some consideration for the situation. I do not think there is much good in our talking to the Minister of Railways. Whatever virtue there may be in the car ferry, it is only in being able to send a loaded car direct to its destination either from Prince Edward Island to the mainland or vice versa. Pending these conditions, however far in the future they may be, to divert the present boats from the route which they now cover, and concentrate all the traffic at an out-of-the-way point, compelling all the travel and all the business to seek that one Tpute, is an unwise and unnecessary thing, and ought not to be permitted. I bespeak from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) that he will see the Minister of Railways and urge him to permit trade and travel to continue their present course until new conditions are provided. Has the department control over freight rates charged by these boats?

Yes, all rates have to be submitted and no changes are made unless they are approved by the department. For a series of years the rates charged by these coast services were kept at about par. They received their subsidies and the rates were the same each year. There may have been some few changes but very few indeed. But, during the past two years there has been an almost universal pressure for some increase in the rates because coal and other costs have increased and it has been a choice between advancing the subsidies and giving a reasonable advance in the rates. The department has taken up each case, and, as well as it could, has come to its decision as to what is a reasonable advance. In some cases applications have been granted, in other cases they have not been and in still other cases the demands have been scaled down. Under present circumstances costs are higher and they have a fair claim for some increase. If there is to be an increase, we do our part by paying the subsidy and asking those who carry on the trade to take their portion of the added cost if there be any through the added rate. It is not an easy thing to do but we have to do it.

I quite appreciate that. Is there any schedule in the department that one could get to show w]hat freight rates these concerns are charging?
A man in my own county, who gets considerable freight over this boat, might like to know what is regarded by the department as a reasonable charge. Could the department furnish anything in that line?

schedule for each one of the services and we have in the department the rates that are charged every year by every one of these subsidized boats.

I again bring this matter to the attention of the minister. The country are paying them a subsidy larger than was ever thought of in the past.
I have made a note of it.
I have never heard anybody say that there were any good results from my former efforts.
