There was another boat from Pictou touching Port Hood, MaTgaree, Mahen, Grand Etang and Cheticamp, tout for some reason the subsidy was taken from the Pictou-Margaree-Cheticamp route and added to the subsidy given to the boat from Mulgrave to Port Hood, Mahen, Margaree, Grand Etang and Cheticamp and Pleasant Bay. The result is that we do not get as good service from Mulgrave on the Intercolonial to ports in Inverness as we did before, owing to the delay caused toy the boat going to Pictou.
It is impossible for one to properly give the two services. I repeat that this boat has no right to go to Pictou at all, but attend to the Mulgrave-Inverness ports. Another if smaller boat should be on the Pictou route as was there before my hon. friend took charge. The steamboat is the only service we have. We have no railway service and surely we should toe expecting improvement in this service Tather than retrogression, as. is now taking place.
It is hard to be the arbiter between two such conflicting interests.
Would the minister mention the ports of call?

The first half dozen names are those at which the schooner calls, and the reason given by the minister for subsidizing the schooner is that the water is very shallow in these harbours. This would look like duplication.

The schooner
calls at a number of ports that are not visited by the steamer.

As I have to leave the House in a few moments I would ask permission to make a few remarks to the committee upon Franco-Camadian trade relations. I tam aware that Canada and France have a steamer service which w.as subsidized by Canada to the extent of $200,000. Will the minister tell the committee the names of the steamers which are performing the service at the present time, and if, generally speaking, they have given satisfaction to the public? I wish to call attention to the fact that the Department of
/

Trade and Commerce, over which my hon. friend presides, should stimulate the manufacturers of Canada to endeavour to get their share of trade in the vast demand that will be made on the various manufacturers of America in the near future, in the reconstruction period into which France is now entering. I have in my hand documents which show that about 729 communes-that is, small villages and towns-have been invaded 'by the Germans. About 200 of them have been relieved since the great drives have been inaugurated by the Allied armies, and, according to the opinion expressed by a member of the French Chamber of Commerce, it is expected that, in a short time, the other communes will also be relieved, and the people of France will then realize that over 50,000 habitations have 'been actually destroyed. Apart from the sympathy which this country has in connection with the terrible disaster which the passage of the Huns in those regions caused, there is a practical view to take of the situation, when all sympathies 'have been given. France will have to reconstruct those hamlets, towns and communes, and she will have to draw on the foreign countries for the raw material. Last year I read to the House a circular which the Chamber of Commerce of Boston and the Board of Trade of New York bad jointly published broadcast in the United States, inviting all the manufacturers to look after the enormous trade which this reconstruction period in France would involve. I told my hon. friend at the time that attention should be paid to that practical side of the question, and I should like to know if anything has been done by his department in that connection. As we have a direct service between Canada and France, it seems to me that it could not be better utilized than by asking each of the manufacturers to encourage that service by the shipping of their goods to France, for the reconstruction of these communes. The trade between Canada and France, I am happy to say, has greatly increased of late years. I find that in 1912 the trade was $14,000,000 in round figures. In 1913, $18,000,000; in 1914, there was an increase of $200,000, making a total of $18,200,000. In 1915 that trade had increased to $22,847,000, and in 1916 to $41,799,951, and I have seen figures which show that up to February, 1917, our trade reached the high water mark of something like $63,000,000, or $65,000,000 for the eleven months of the current fiscal year. This means that France is an excellent client of Canada, and that we should not maintain 
that trade for war purposes only, but that we should try to capture that market for the years of reconstruction, which will come very shortly. Bight or ten years ago a committee of very distinguished Frenchmen was formed. One of the most prominent members of that committee was Monsieur Gabriel Hanotaux, former Minister of Foreign Affairs in France. He and Monsieur Ribot, the President of the Council in France, were the fathers of the alliance between Russia and France. This committee, viewing with alarm the strides made by the Germans on the various foreign markets, and the attention paid by the German traders to North and South American trade, formed an association called Franee-Amerique. It comprised all the prominent friends of the United States, Canada, Argentina, Brazil, and some other of the southern republics. They have their head office in Paris. They publish a monthly magazine called France-Ameri-que, and this review of very high order is devoted chiefly to the promotion of good fellowship between the Allied nations, and also to the development of better trade relations with these nations. This committee sent a delegation to Canada a few years ago, which visited Montreal and Quebec, after having visited the United States. On its return to Paris the committee published a little book which I hold in my hand, about the possibilities of trade between France and Canada. The contents of that book are most interesting. I ask my hon. friend to communicate with this committee in Paris, through the Commissioner for Canada in France, Monsieur Philippe Roy, and through the French Consul General in Montreal, Monsieur Bonin, who has worked so conscientiously and so unsparingly since he has been in Montreal for the enlargement of trade relations between France and Canada. Through the Comite France-AmeHque the minister will find the natural channel his department requires abroad for making known in France the resources of Canada, and at the same time he will get, through the review published by that comite, an advertisement of the greatest advantage.
On two occasions I have spoken of the project launched a year ago by a committee of French and Canadian business men for the equipment of exhibition trains, one touring the principal cities of France with the staple products of Canada, and the other touring our country from ocean to ocean with the staple products of France.

A voluminous correspondence has been exchanged between Senator Beaubien and the minister on this subject, and the minister encouraged the movement as far as it lay in his power to do so. I have the correspondence before me. I have here the answer the minister made to Senator Beaubien, and although the project for the time being fell through because of the dire necessities of war, I hope that at the earliest opportunity, this project will receive the attention of the minister. The manufacturers of Toronto and Montreal have manifested a deep interest in it. Our four railway systems, the Intercolonial, thanks to the good-will of the Minister of Railways and Canals, the Grand Trunk, the 9 p.m. Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern have agreed to give the trains free access over their systems. I have here the letters which have been sent to Senator Beaubien on the subject, and the following firms are willing to favour the scheme: The Desbarats Printing Company, Limited, Montreal; The Phoenix Bridge and Iron Works, Ltd., Montreal. This company understand that in the reconstruction period in France our structural steel will be sorely required by the communes which have been so heavily devastated. Then there is the Roland Paper Company, Limited, Montreal. France is already a large consumer of Canadian pulp, and we must encourage that trade as much as possible. I know a firm, the Chicoutimi Pulp and Paper -Company, which had some large contracts with the publishers of Le Petit Parisien, a paper which has a circulation of about a million a day. That journal is supplied with its paper by a Canadian firm. This is one instance; I could name others:	The Canada Linseed
Oil Mills Co., Montreal, Laurentide Company, Limited, Montreal, J. & T. Bell, Limited, Montreal, The Steel Company of Canada, Limited, Montreal, S. H. Ewing and Sons, coffees, -spices, corks, wholesale teas and general commission -merchants, Montreal, The William Rutherford and Sons Co., Ltd-., Montreal, Cluett, Peabody and Company, Inc., Montreal, Charles E. Frost & 'Company, Pharmaceutical Chemists, Montreal, The Montreal Cottons, Ltd., Valleyfield, B. J. Coghlin Company, Ltd., railway supplies, etc., Montreal.
The various boards of trade in Canada and in France have also given their support to that project. I quite agree with the minister that at present we -must abandon the idea of having an exhibition on wheels, but I hope the project will not be shelved
in the files of the department. We must, by all means, maintain the trade between France and -Canada at the figure, namely, $60,000,000, which it has reached. It would be -regrettable, indeed, if, with a treaty between France and Canada -and with a steamer service between Havre and Montreal -we should revert to the days when we hardly did any business with that magnificent country, the pride of the world. This war has awakened the sympathies and also the commercial activities of our people, -and in the years we shall have in France one of out foremost commercial Allies.

I have listened with interest to the statement of my hon. friend. We have no subsidized -service running now between Canada and France, . nor have we had one since the first yeaT of the war. Conditions make it impossible for boats to be put on that service. There was a -statutory provision under which we paid a subsidy to the boats of the Allan line before the war commenced.
The statement that my hon. friend has made with reference to the closer acquaintanceship between France and England is very apt, and we look for results frp-m it. We do not look upon it as an acquaintanceship generated for war purposes only, and to continue only during the war. We believe that as they become better acquainted with us and with our resources, and as we become better acquainted with them and with the particular wants to which we may cater, the foundation for an expansion of trade will -be laid on a better basis than ever before. But after all, a department, ever so wide awake a department as that of Trade and Commerce, cannot go beyond a certain point. The merchants themselves, the producers and the business men, must take advantage of their opportunities and pu-sh the interchange and exchange of articles between the two countries. A very instructive letter appeared in the Bulletin a week ago from our commissioner in Paris, which I would advise my hon. friend to read if he has not already done so, as I think it struck the nail right on the head. In a word it amounted to this: there is plenty of trade in France for the future if Canadian business men will look after it, but it will not take to itself wings and fly 0-ver here; it needs the nurture and care and enterprise and activity of the men who are interested on this side of the world. The United States has awakened to great activity in thought, and in planning to cater to the wants of the reconstruction period, but in so far as France is concerned, the
COMMON^
letter goes on to say that the people of the United States have not made much more progress- than we have, and for the same reason-they have not banded themselves together to look after the possibilities of the future.	.
The $50,000,000 to $60,000,000 trade that my hon. friend has spoken of is of course only a war trade, and we shall only be laying up disappointment for ourselves if we expect that figure to be kept up after the war. It will sag, but afterwards it will rise again if we look after the .opportunities which I am sure are open to us. France will need the natural resources that we can supply, and as her Ally we shall be given a sentimental advantage in France. At the present time negotiations are proceeding for the supply of a large amount of lumber from Canada for reconstruction purposes after the war. Correspondence is taking place with my own department, and I hope it will come to much, but it will not do so unless producers on this side take advantage of their opportunities. It is true that the producers of Canada for the last three years, arid at no time more than now, have had their hands and hearts full in doing what was necessary to be done for the war, and it has been difficult-I acknowledge the difficulty-to switch them from the absolutely necessary work of the war and turn their thoughts and activities to planning for conditions after the war, but they are thinking more about it than ever before. No one knows, however, when the war will end, and no one knows what conditions will be when the war does end, and it is practically impossible for them to lay definite plans until the conditions that will prevail are more definitely known than at the present time. It is a case largely of watching and waiting, not simply waiting, but planning in- thought, if not in actual outlay and equipment, for the seeming possibilities of trade after the war.
The project of an exhibition on wheels is a lively and up-to-date project; it is a good project, but at the present time it is absolutely impossible of achievement because of transport conditions in France, and transport conditions here would not favour it. The project has to go into the category of those things that are not out of sight , simply because they are not being carried out. Here, again, we shall have to watch and wait for the proper opportunity.

In connection with the reconstruction period in France, it was suggested to the minister, I think, that a 
number of ready-built houses, such as in my younger days we used to see in Ottawa, should be exhibited in Paris. Has anything been done along that line?

The matter was brought to my attention, -and I took it up with the department and had the woodworkers plan certain houses. After these plans were made it was thought better- and -under my advice it was done-to .send the plans to Paris to have them thoroughly looked into -and vised, as it were, by governmental authority, acting either directly or through a committee. That was done, and we received modified plans from them for two or three different styles of what we would call shacks, to be used temporarily until more permanent buildings could be erected. In every case their plan called for a more elaborate and more costly building than we had planned. Our buildings would -cost from $75 to $100, but with the improvements, coverings and the like of that, suggested toy the French authorities, they would cost considerably more. However, a number of houses were constructed and I got transport for them free of charge to Paris, where they were on exhibition in the Champs Elyse'es. I myself saw them when I was over there last summer. They had the name of Canada on them, and served to show not only our plan of construction for temporary buildings of this kind, but our materials as well, and they were seen by a great many people. [DOT] But the war has gone on much longer than anybody thought it would, and although we know now what they want and though the plans are in the hands of the woodworkers of Canada, not much is being done at present. They, too, I suppose, are awaiting the proper time. What works directly against -them is the absolute impossibility of getting transport for goods. [DOT]

I think that the question of our trade with France is one of the most important subjects to be discussed in this House. The ideas that prevail in Canada as to what will be required in France after the war is over are- largely erroneous. For instance, it is expected by many that immediately after -the war we are going to be called upon to send large shipments- of lumber and ready-made houses to France. Having lived in the war zone, I have some idea of what the requirements there are likely to be; also, I am conversant with the building trade. The building material used in France is almost entirely brick. When a farmer wants brick to build a house he

simply goes into his fields, builds a kiln, and makes his brick. The lumber used for the roof consists of limbs from the trees in the fields, usually elm. The timbers for the building are the same. The flooring and roof is tile, which the farmer makes out of clay, as he does his brick. Consequently, the wood products that we shall need to send to France will be doorsr window sash and some flooring. For doors and window sash we are likely to find a ready sale. We should get patterns from France in order that we may be in a position to supply what they will require. Then there is hardware.
And structural steel-

Yes, I wish to deal with all these matters. I had these things under observation when I was there, and I think that after the war there will be a large market for builders' hardware such as locks, hinges, aiid other things, usually of a cheap kind. In France, most of these articles that have been destroyed by the Germans were made by the local blacksmiths, and we ought to be able to supply the French people With a cheaper line of articles	suitable	for	their
building purposes. As to structural material, it is to 'be assumed that after the war France will have recovered her iron and steel works, and will be able to supply for her own use large quantities of rails and of structural material. But many bridges of the old regime, stone bridges, will be replaced with 'bridges of steel, and a great deal of structural material will he used in France in that way after the war. Figures show that already a large trade has sprung up between Canada and France, and it is not altogether a war trade. Many articles of iron and steel manufactured in Canada are shipped to France, as well as certain textiles and articles of wood. The concern that has taken charge of this trade in France is the Hudson's Bay Company. That company has something like forty or fifty ships carrying goods from the United States and Canada to France. So far that company has given a preference to Canadian goods. But the United States is lending large sums of money to France, and I notice that these loans are made on condition that the purchases to be made with the money shall be confined to the United States. I have not observed that the Canadian Government is lending money and in this way promoting the purchase of goods here for France. France had already borrowed large sums in the United States, but without any string on the money, with the
result that she was able to place large orders in Canada. I know this because I know of one concern which had an order of half a million dollars from France, not of a war character, but, as I may say, of a semi-war character. But we have reached the highest point in that trade. There does not seem to be any arrangement made for the exchange, the money, to continue the purchase of these goods in Canada from now on, and those who have been manufacturing goods for France and have been looking forward to a continuance of the trade will find this business falling off within the next two or three months. The purchasing, I understand, is taken out of the hands of the parties who had it and is given to the Imperial Munitions Board, which has now virtually come under the rule of Washington, and the purchases for France must be confined to American goods. Therefore, I do not think that Canada need look for more than eight or ten millions of dollars' worth of business with France next year unless something is done. This is to 'be regretted.
I would strongly urge upon the Government the necessity of looking thoroughly into this French trade question. It is not altogether a matter of shells and munitions. It is a valuable trade and can be continued after the war if the necessary credits and exchange are provided. Therefore, those in Canada who are manufacturing for France-and I know a number of them-need not, I think, look forward to more business after the next two or three months when their present contracts expire, because they are faced with the fact that purchases made for France from now on must be made in the United States, because the money is being provided by the United States. I wonder whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce has taken this matter into consideration. If not, I would urge him to .look into it to see if *some arrangement cannot be made so that the French Government may participate in the credit here with the British Government, so that this trade, which is important, may continue not only now but after the war.
'Mr. LOGGIE:	The minister referred to
the fact that the subsidy is not used by the Allan Bine. I am sure he will recall the fact that boats of the Allan Line that loaded at Montreal did not load their full cargo for Havre but after discharging at Havre, went on to London and did not stop long at Havre because of the congestion and the difficulty of unloading cargo. Has any effort been made to procure the service in

a different way? For instance, if a monthly steamer were to start from Halifax and go via New York, or Portland, or both, having in view a full cargo for Havre, would not that meet an existing demand? I am informed that several steamers loaded partly with Canadian military stores, and also carrying commercial go.ods to some extent, went from Portland. But these sailings were known to very few of the *mercantile people. I can understand the reason for that, as these vessels were carrying military stores. But I think that in the interests of the commercial world it would be worth while for the department to find out if it would not be practicable to have two or three sailings start from Halifax calling at Portland and New York, and then to Havre with a full cargo. I am quite sure that there was not the slightest difficulty in procuring full cargoes because I know that goods were held up in New York for months last year and practically all the goods that were forwarded from the Maritime Provinces to France went by New York.
Mr.. CURRIE: Does the hon. gentleman not know that there was a ship sailing for France each day nearly all last summer?
Were they of the French line?
I do not know what the name of the company was that was operating the ships, but they sent out a ship every day from Montreal last summer.
I know that there are ships in the employ of the Government sailing from Montreal to Havre, but these ships' will not carry commercial goods.
They did.
Then I am wrongly advised. I would like to know to whom to apply, as I am interested in applications for tonnage. *

Why not apply to the parties who have these boats in charge? Nearly all of these ships are chartered by the Hudson's Bay Company, and if the hon. gentleman would apply for tonnage I am satisfied that they would let him have it.
I will be very glad to do so, and I shall certainly use the information which my hon. friend has given me.
If it is correct.

Yes, if it is correct. I fancy that we will find that it has a little flaw in it when we come down to the busi-
ness end of it. But we look to the minister to keep up communication between Canada and France. The minister suggested that it was not possible after war was declared. I know his difficulties. I know there was a ship on the sea bound for Havre at the time war was declared, and that the cargo was discharged at London and held a long time there before it was sent across the channel. The sailings to France were discontinued. If the minister will have his ships fully loaded when they set out for Havre it will help to solve the trouble. The difficulty with the Allan line boats is that they have not been loaded for Havre but for London, and they have taken some cargo for Havre/ They do not want to lose time by calling at Havre. If the steamers had been fully loaded there would not have been that difficulty. I hope the minister will find some boats that will enable us to have a sailing once or twice a month during the summer with a full cargo for Havre. They have the right to call at one port after they leave Halifax, to call at New York and then to sail for France. I am not sure whether they have a right to call at Portland. If the minister will look into it I will be very much obliged.

The statement made by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) to the effect that under existing conditions the whole control of purchases for war needs in France is to be vested in our American friends is a statement of very great import. I see no reason why there should not be a conference between our Government and the French and British Governments in regard to this whole question of purchases of this character. We see French and English commissions coming to the United States, we see conferences in regard to financial matters and arrangements being made for providing food supplies of all kinds. You find a British minister stating in the Imperial House of Commons that they are relying on the United States for their food supply. Why should they not be relying on this country for their food supply in regard to production, and why should not France, as far as our industries may permit, have arrangements made so that Canada might take some part in the rebuilding of France just the same as under existing circumstances we are told the United States are to do? I hope the minister will be able to give us some assurance that a condition of that kind is not being permitted to exist and, if it does exist, steps should be taken to remedy it immediately.

Has the minister anything to suggest as a way out of the difficulty which we meet in sending goods to France while the war is going on? I am sure that when the war is over the matter will be adjusted but in the meantime something might be done by the Government.

I think care ought to be taken before statements are made or criticisms are offered that the sources of information are correct. At this time there is a multiplicity of statements made as to what is going to be done iand what is being done. There is a multitude of projects sent in from various sources to the two Houses of Congress in the shape of bills but no man on earth knows what the shape of the matter will be when it gets out of Congress. I do not bestow very much time or attention upon Bills that are merely introduced into committees of the two Houses of Congress, and which are waiting for discussion and ultimate action. It is a peculiar thing that in all that has been going on since the second day of April, and in all the preparation that has been made in order to put powers into the hands of the administration of the United States, up to the present moment only three important Bills have really become law. One is the Loan Bill, another the Bill for selective conscription and the third is the one which has been passed just a day or so ago and which is known as the Espionage Bill. The name, however, does not give very much of an indication of what the Bill is. The essence of the Bill is to confer a power upon the administrative authorities to control exports from the United States, and in that way to put into their hands a power of blockade which is the most effective which can be established with reference to the Central Powers in Europe.
The powers with regard to censorship which were originally in the Bill were stricken out?

The proposition which was made was changed in the first Bill and then the section of the first Bill which was passed was tooi wide to suit Congress and the extreme espionage provisions of the Bill were stricken out. But there are considerable powers of supervision, or of espionage as it is called, still remaining in the Bill. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) says that he has noticed that in the British House of Parliament statements are made that Britain looks to the United States for their food supply.
Statements are also made by the leader in that House that Great Britain and the Allies look to Canada as well as to the United States for their supplies. I should not like the impression to go out, and I am sure that my hon. friend would not, that the British people were saying in their Parliament that they looked to the United States foT their supplies and left Canada out.
I was speaking about understandings, following my hon. friend from Simcoe.

There is this to he remembered: when we want to do anything here in war time we have a more speedy way of doing it. Under the War Measures Act, almost any power can be taken and can be exercised by the Government for war purposes and under war pressure. An Order in Council gives the power,'and you go on and exercise it. In the United States there is no such thing as an Order in Council or a War Measures Act. When a .state of war was declared in the United States, the President and the secretaries of the different departments had no more power in these respects and could get no more power than any outsider, and they cannot get that power until it is conferred in every separate instance and in every separate line by Acts of Congress. It is these Acts of Congress for which the Administration is waiting and has been waiting, in order to organize, the several departments of work. Take the matter of food regulation and food supplies. That bill is still before Congress. It is being debated, it has not yet been passed. It has been before Congress for ten or fourteen days. It is expected that it will be passed in a few days. When it is in so far as powers are given, then, the Administration will be able to use those powers. The French mission and the British mission visited Washington and conferences were had with the United States Administration. Lines of effort and co-operation were discussed and principles were laid down and in course of time agreed to, and they will be adhered to; but up to the present time, in most particulars, the Administration has not received the powers that are necessary to enable them to act. Cooperation between Canada and the United States, thorough co-operation between the Alliee and their commissions, and the United States, is what is being aimed at and is what I believe will be carried out.
With reference to the purchase of sup-

plies for the Allies, Canada's resources, I am quite sure, will be called upon for everything that she can possibly supply. I do not know that there is a staple food product that Canada can make or produce this year, after she has served her own people, and has a surplus, that will not be exigency required by the Allies, and every ounce of exportable wheat and flour made therefrom is required and will be asked for by the Allied powers through their buying commission. So that we are not being left out in the cold in any possible iway. Neither do I know, I have no authority for saying -if I were asked I would say exactly the opposite-that all the money which is loaned to Great Britain or to France or to the other Allies must be expended in the United States of America. There is this fact to be considered, that Britain's advance contracts made in the United States were tremendously large, -and I believe that almost every cent of the loans so far made to Great Britain has gone to pay for advances that were already made in that country. To that extent, if the purchases were in the United States and the debt was owed for them in the United States, those moneys would go, of course, to clear off that indebtedness. But I have yet to learn that there is any absolute string that is placed upon the expenditure of the money. Naturally most of it will be expended in the United States of America by the Allies v ho desire to obtain supplies.
With reference to transit from this country to France, there are not, as I have said, any subsidized services-there have not been since the war. Havre became, almost immediately after the outbreak of war, a port so congested that it was almost impossible for a merchant vessel to get any service there, and even up to the present time it is a great British seaport, and supplies and munitions and equipments fqr war flood and congest it. The Hudson Bay Company has been, and still is, the agent of France, to a large extent, in buying in this country, but the Hudson Bay Company with its ships, either owned or chartered- and there are a good many of them -has . been buying for the French Government, and it is the articles that the French Government needs that have the first place, if I am not wrongly informed, almost the. total claim upon these vessels.
I have had man after man and company after company ask my good offices to get commercial freight on the Hudson Bay Company's vessels, but I have not succeeded in doing so because the claims of the 
French Government were paramount and they had to be. In one case I did get a consignment put upon one of those boats, but it was because the French Government saw that that particular consignment was almost absolutely necessary for French agriculturists, and so they made some room on one of the vessels in order that that shipment might go forward.
Two countries like Canada and the United States, with their basic products almost the same, taking food into consideration, must act in conjunction with each other; a border line of three thousand miles, with producers and farmers on each side, has to be looked at in these matters. The consumers in the United States have just as large stomachs and just as big appetites as consumers in Canada, and it is certain that, in all the regulation of prices that may take place, the vast mass of consumers in the United States will be considered as being a very vital factor. On the other hand, production is just as necessary for the United States at this hour as it is for Canada, and if anything it is a little more necessary. Production must be looked at in the fixing of prices as well as consumption, and you must strike a happy medium which give price enough to attract productive enterprise and yet prices not unreasonable, under all the circumstances, for the consumer.
I't is absolute folly for any one of us to imagine that we can appoint a food controller, and that he can go into the market in Montreal, Toronto, or anywhere else and fix prices at his arbitrary discretion, without having regard to supply and demand and the conditions that are world-wide today. If we try to bolster ourselves up with such a remedy we shall be trusting to a quack remedy, and shall only meet with disappointment. In this world there are forces which no mayor of a city, and no man seated on a nail keg and talking to his fellows of the enormous prices that are demanded, is going to have very much influence on. The results are 'being motived by world causes, and these are* as the deep currents of the sea. Storage and speculation-are but scum and froth upon the surface, not to be allowed if they can be kept off, to be sedulously looked into, restrained and restricted; but to-day we are called upon to pay high prices because of the 'basic conditions of the times in which we live, supervening upon three years of the most disastrous and widely destructive war that history has ever recorded.

The minister has scarcely answered the question put to him

in respect of possible sales of goods 'by-Canada to France. If I understood the question aright, it was whether in the event of Canada selling goods to France the Government had in contemplation any means of financing international transactions. The member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) emphasized the desirability of trade between France and Canada, but the weakness of his argument was that he suggested no way by which France could pay Canada for goods purchased. The truth is that if tomorrow Canada sold to France $200,000,000 of structural steel there is no way by which France could pay for it, except by Canada, or some one on 'her behalf, making a loan to France, and paying for the commercial transaction with the proceeds of the loan. The United States is selling to France and England tremendous supplies of goods, but everybody knows that this is only possible because the United States is willing to lend, and is lending, to these countries the money with which to pay for these goods. While it is very desirable that we take advantage of the possible trade open to us in France, for instance, during the reconstruction days which are soon to come, still the wishing of it does not bring the trade. The person suggesting the proposition should propose some way of financing the transaction. It is a matter, I think, to which the Government should give some consideration. It is very desirable that we should have a share of the European trade which will be coming to this side of the Atlantic after the cessation of the war. Our factories will then have ceased their work upon, munitions and war contracts, and it would be very disastrous if our largest industries were closed down- for the want of orders. If we can bring to this country contracts from the European countries amounting to some hundreds of millions of dollars in order to keep our factories open and our labour market busy, that certainly is desirable, and I think, if possible, the Government should assist our industries to make these sales abroad. I do not know at the moment just how it could be done, because Canada perhaps could hardly afford to borrow money at the present time for such purposes, but she might do so temporarily, and she might dispose, in the United States or elsewhere, of these securities which France, or other (purchasing countries, would gladly give to the Cana. dian Government. In that way, Canadian exporters might be paid for orders which came to this side of the water from the 148
European countries. If the minister is desirous of developing this class of trade with European countries after the war, it seems to me that he must consider the question of assisting our manufacturers in arranging the financial transactions which are incident to such commercial exchange of goods. If this cannot be done, there is not much use keeping the elaborate machine going in the Department of Trade and Commerce. It may be educative, but it can bring no trade to the country. My impression is that I have seen in the press, on several occasions, the statement that the minister has had many interviews with Canadians relative to the export of their products to the Aliied countries now and after the cessation of war. I would like to inquire from him if that matter was ever placed before the manufacturers by the minister, or did they place it before him for consideration?

I do not know that I can answer all my hon. friend's questions. When this war is over, and the exhausting processes of the war have had their effects, I do not know what will happen with regard to the purchase of new and necessary material for the reconstruction of the damaged and ravaged countries that have passed through the war. We know the course of events at the present time. The Allies, in so far as their resources and credit went, financed themselves as long as they could. They then very largely had recourse to Great Britain, and Great Britain financed them, and is helping to finance them to-day, and, on the whole, has financed them to a most tremendous extent, as my hon. friend knows. Now, the great nation which has lately gone into the war, with her resources undiminished by the ravages of war, has all the advantages which have come from business resulting from the war, and is looked to, to give credit, and she is giving credit. No one likes to say that France or Great Britain or Italy is exhausted. Those countries are not exhausted, but they have gone through a tremendous process of exhaustion during the three years of the war, and financially they are in a very tense state of strain. What will happen after the United States has given its loans to the aid of the Allies to the extent that it can, and after the war has been finished and after the reconstruction takes place and new material has to 'be secured, is a problem most difficult of solution. One thing of two and, maybe, two things will take place.



first that, instead of reconstruction going ahead at a bounding pace after the war ceases, it may have, by sheer necessity, to go ahead at a very moderate rate, and people will probably have to live for many years in less comfort and with fewer appliances and equipments than they had before; secondly, that the actual necessities in some way or another must be had, and the Government and financial institutions will have to come to the rescue in so far as these necessaries must *be bought. Take Canada at the present time, and to turn to the *question of my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean): is there any way by which Canada can finance the producing interests of the country, manufacturers, for instance, in order to enable them to finance Allied countries which are not able to meet the payments at present? My hon. friend has to take into account that money markets are pretty well closed to Canada at the present time. She cannot make loans in Great Britain; on the contrary she has advanced many millions of dollars to finance orders that Great Britain has placed in this country, but there is a limit to Canada's capability for doing that for what is sold to Great Britain or to France, because Canada has to take up and to take that burden almost entirely upon heT own shoulders from this time on, however long or short the war may be. That makes it difficult for the Government to arrange financial strength in order to protect large sales to be made to Allied countries and payments to be made to manufacturers without their having to wait a long time for them. The banks do their share in that respect, and they must be relied upon with their combinations to bear a large share of the burden. It depends on how far the banks can go along that line.
It would be well to have some experts study the matter so as to anticipate the future.
My hon. friend can rest assured that these matters have been and are being studied. It is easy to study them; it is much more difficult to find a solution.

The vital point that I
raised has not .been answered; that is to say, that orders that are placed now upon this money that is being borrowed by France in the United States, must be .placed in the United States. I know for a fact that many orders in this country for France and Great Britain are being held up on that account. Of all the business that we have done with

Great Britain and France in respect to the war-and according to our returns we have turned out millions of dollars worth of munitions-fully two-thirds of the money went to the United States for the raw material. Fully two-thirds of the steel and copper that has been sold to the Allies by Canada, has come from the United States, and Canada's money has paid for that. Therefore, when the United States trade papers all announce distinctly that every dollar of this loan that the Allies are getting from the United States, must be spent in the United States, that is an unfriendly act, and this 'Government should take steps to ascertain whether it is true, because we are just as much entitled to some business from that money as is the United States. It should be a free loan.
It is the money of the United States.

The United States lends
that money on the understanding that it must be spent in the United States and not in Canada, nor in the Argentine Republic.
It was borrowed on that condition.
We have had a very great deal of theory and cloud navigation for the last hour or so, and perhaps we had better come down to earth again.
Perhaps we had better come hack to the Estimates.

I do not want the line to be drawn the moment I have something to say. The minister was the worst sinner of all. He went careering all over the country, .and I must ask him to permit me to do a little careering. The hon. member for Simcoe has brought out a point which ' is rather against the minister. In his judgment the minister is a man full of capacity and ability, but he will not do anything. Now, there is some excuse for a man not doing anything who has no ability, but no excuse at all for a man at the head of a department who has, as the hon. member say3, both ability and capacity. I was very glad to read the Order in Council that the minister laid on the Table yesterday; that was a practical step. The Order in Council says that Mr. Magrath is to be fuel controller. That has a very restricted meaning. By fuel we usually understand fire wood, or what is used for domestic purposes, but the Order in Council is much more comprehensive in its scope. It deals with power of every kind that is produced from steam or coal, as well as with domestic fuel. I notice that some months ago the minister called before him the coal managers of the different parts of Canada, particularly of the Maritime Provinces, and he has the advantage of the knowledge he gained in that way. I come from a very large coal centre and know something about coal mining, and about what a mine may ordinarily be supposed to produce. A manager may say that such an amount is the full capacity of his mine, (but if you can show him where he is going to make money he will produce more. If the minister would give the coal companies of Canada, and of Nova Scotia particularly, a fixed price for every pound of coal they produce up to their utmost capacity the mines of Nova

Scotia would be producing four million instead of three million tons a year, and so on throughout the country. The Government would be taking no risk, because every pound of coal they bought they could readily dispose of. But the great thing is to hold out to the coal companies an inducement to produce an article for which there is the greatest possible demand, and for which there will be the greatest possible necessity. Bather than find fault with the minister for this appointment, I think the task he has imposed on Mr. Magrath is too much for any one man; he has more than he can accomplish. The fuel controller should not ask the coal managers, how much coal have you in your bank? How much did you produce yesterday, and how much will you produce tomorrow? He should be empowered by the minister to say to them, "Produce as much as you like. We will give you a fixed price for every pound you produce." The minister should adopt a policy similar to that followed by the Government at the inception of the munitions industry, when the manufacturers were told to produce as much as they liked, and would be given a fixed price for a certain number of years which would cover the cost of their plant and allow a very substantial profit besides. The minister need not be afraid that he will have coal on his hands because he will be taking gold out of the ground. I again want to impress upon him the necessity of holding out inducements to the large coal companies to produce to their utmost capacity. In the Order in Council it is stated that only 200,000 tons of coal could be got in Nova Scotia to meet the demands of Montreal and other places. That is mere folly. It is ridiculous to mention such a figure as 200,000 tons in connection with the tremendous coal mines in the Island of Cape Breton and Pictou, particularly in the Island of Cape Breton. I can assure the minister that if he will hold out such an inducement of this kind, the coal companies will have no difficulty in providing all the coal he wants.
Referring to item 183, at what points does the steamer call?

At Chatham, lower Newcastle, Loggieville, Oak Point, [DOT]Church Point, Escuminae, Neguac, and Mills Point Wharf on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, and at Chatham, Lower Newcastle, Loggieville, Oak Point, Baie-du-Tin, Church Point and Neguac on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

Steam service .between Riviere du Loup, Tadoussac and other north shore ports, $6,000.
Winter steam service between Riviere du Loup, Tadoussac and other St. Lawrence ports, $8,0-00.
Winter steam service between St. Catherines Bay and Tadoussac, $3,500.

It has always been
hard for me to understand why the Minister of Trade and Commerce was so quick to listen to politicians when he entered into that last contract for winter and summer navigation between Riviere du Loup, Tadoussac, and North shore. Perhaps he is not aware that the Trans-St. Laurent Navigation Company, of Fraserville, was really the pioneer of winter navigation, on the lower St. Lawrence. If he comes to Riviere du Loup, where he will be well received, he will find that a little boat called the Mahone has done a really great service on the St. Lawrence, especially in its winter trips made to Seven islands for the relief of the people there. I thought at the time that, in view of what this company had done, it would be better treated by the department and by the minister. But, unfortunately, .politics carried weight, even in so serious a matter as this. In 1912, Mr. Berube was elected to the local legislature for Temiscouata, and he happens to be a Conservative. Being unfriendly to the management of the company, he started at once to oppose it. Then there was the hon. member for Chicoutimi and Saguenay (Mr. Girard) a Conservative member on the North shore. With these two warring against it, it is no wonder that the poor company was killed. The contract with that company was cancelled and a contract was made with the Quebec and Levis Ferry Boat Company. At the time I warned the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) that the boat they proposed to use, which had been built principally for the ferry crossing between Quebec and Levis, could never stand the strain of the trip between Riviere du Loup and Tadoussac and the North shore. I never thought that this would be so quickly proven. But in the winter of 1915, the boat went op a rock on Red Island at the mouth of the Saguenay Tiver. She was a total loss, and if there were no lives lost it is due to the fact that this little boat, the Mahone, went to the rescue and rendered good service. The contractors then sent out the Queen, and two months afterwards she was sunk in St. Catherines Bay, on the north shore. This is what happened to the company that stepped into the place of the Trans-St. Laurent Navigation Company, of Fraser-

ville. I think the minister realizes that if there is a place below Quebec where we need steamer communication it is between Tadoussac and Riviere du Loup. I believe the amount appropriated is sufficient for ordinary circumstances-these three services represent a total of $17,500. But since these two boats disappeared we have been without means of crossing. Tenders were called for, and I believe that the Trans-St. Laurent Navigation Company sent in tenders. But, if I am well informed, their tender was higher than the amount placed in the Estimates. This, no doubt, accounted for the refusal of the minister to give the contract. At present we have no service at all. I hope that the minister will try to arrange that, even if a larger sum is necessary, the tender of the Trans-St. Laurent Navigation Company shall foe accepted and their boat may foe placed on the line.
How long did they have the contract?

For many years, up to 1914 I think. Perhaps the minister may say that the boat is too small, or that she has been condemned. That may be true so far as the winter traffic is concerned. But he will see by the report of the commissioner who was sent down there that the boat could have been allowed to make trips in the winter, carrying freight only and no passengers. If I am well informed there is a man who wishes to place a gasoline launch on this route between Riviere du Loup and Tadoussac. I do not know what kind of a boat it is, nor what is its capacity, but I am told that this man, Mr. Lajoie, of Chicoutimi, is recommended by the hon. member for Chicoutimi and Saguenay. Well, even a small boat would be better than none, and I hope that the minister will find a way to give us a service between Riviere du Loup and Tadoussac, first in the summer, and then in the winter time.

I am not thoroughly clear in my own mind with regard to the steps that have been taken in this matter, but my impression is that the vessel that was there was condemned and consequently we were unable to employ her. We require a certificated vessel. Then came the difficulty of getting another vessel.
The boat was not condemned as a freighter, but it was condemned under the pretext that it was not safe for passengers. You can employ a boat as a freighter without allowing passengers to go on board.

Yes, but we subsidize for both freight and passengers, and as it was impossible for them to carry passengers because of the condemnation, we did not feel that we could subsidize the boat. There has always been the difficulty of the exceedingly small amount of freight to be carried. Take, for instance, the route between Rivifere du Loup, Tadoussac and St. Lawrence ports, for which there was $8,000 subsidy. The number of trips made in 1916 was 29, and the amount of freight carried was 42 tons. That was about one and a half tons per trip. It is a very small amount, of tons per trip. It is very small amount of pay for it. You could buy that tonnage over and over again for $8,000, and if the boat could not carry passengers it seemed too much to pay. We asked for tenders, but the tenders were still higher, and in some cases it became impossible to get a boat. I will look into it and read the remarks that my hon. friend has made.

The minister says that he could not subsidize a boat condemned as far as the passenger service is. concerned. I am informed that the steamer Amelia, plying between the mainland and the Magdalen islands, was condemned last fall as a passenger steamer.
Sir -GEORGE FOSTER: No, she has a certificate and always has had. She would not be allowed to run without a certificate.

Would the minister go back to item No. 191:
Steam service between Prince Edward Island and Cape Breton and Newfoundland, $16,500.
How often will the trips be made, and at what ports in Prince Edward Island will the boats call?

I think it is the same as last year:
Regular sailings every fortnight between Summerside, P.E.I., and St. Johns, Nfld., calling each way at Charlottetown, P.E.I., at Sydney, N.S., and, if so required by the minister, calling on outward voyages only at Souris, P.E.I., and North Sydney, N.S.
What is the name of the boat?
The Sable Island.

I have had complaints from my town about that boat because when going to Sydney she passes our port and does not call. If she had to go farther to call there might be some excuse for it, but in going in and coming out she has to pass North Sydney and if she brings freight

for North Sydney she leaves it at Sydney and it has to be reshipped to North Sydney. Some arrangement should be made by which this boat would regularly call at North Sydney.
Progress reported.
On the motion of Sir George Foster for the adjournment of the House:
What business will be taken up to-morrow?
I do not know what arrangement has been made by the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition as to the Military Service Bill.
I think it is not coming up until next week.
Not to-morrow?
Not to-morrow.

subtopic: PROPOSED MOTION BY HON. GEO. P.

speechtext:
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM: I wish to notify the Government that at an appropriate time I will move the following or a similar resolution:
That in the opinion of this House it is desirable that steps should be taken forthwith by the Government to provide that accumulated wealth should contribute immediately and effectively to the cost of the war, and that all agricultural, industrial, transportation and natural resources of Canada should be organized forthwith so as to ensure the greatest possible assistance to the Empire in the war and to reduce the cost of living to the Canad dian people.
